newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich - humbler, gentler U.S. House speaker.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich - humbler, gentler U.S. House speaker.

text.p: Newt Gingrich's re-election as speaker of the House of Representatives opens Act Two of a saga that has changed him from conquering hero to chastened survivor waving olive branches.

Humbled by ethical breaches now hanging over his head, scarred by political blunders, the conservative 53-year-old Georgian -- with the muffin face and ink-dot eyes beloved of political cartoonists -- retained his post only after fervent wooing and arm-twisting of House Republican colleagues.
In a vote he barely won after a few of his troops deserted him anyway, the old political brawler accepted re-election in a most un-Gingrichian way: he apologised.

"Let me say to the entire House that ... to the degree I was too brash, too self-confident or too pushy, I apologise," he told the assembled bipartisan House. "To whatever degree in any way that I have brought controversy or inappropriate attention to the House, I apologise."

It was a far cry from the cocky, combative political pit bull who took the speakership by right two years ago as architect of an election triumph that gave Republicans their first two-house congressional majorities in 40 years.

He was, then, Time magazine's latest "Man of the Year" cover boy. He was much discussed as a potential 1996 Republican presidential candidate. He was, as his supporters loved to chant on sight of him, "Newt! Newt! Newt!"

He remains a political force, able and shrewd. But it is an admittedly sadder, undoubtedly wiser Newt Gingrich now trying to hold onto the third-highest elective office in the United States after the presidency and vice presidency.
True, he succeeded in becoming the first Republican elected speaker in successive Congresses since 1929.
But he will also become -- in about two weeks, after House disciplinary procedures that begin Wednesday -- the first speaker ever to face punishment by vote of the House.

The immediate cause of Gingrich's woes are the findings of a House ethics subcommittee -- which he has conceded "with great sadness -- that he failed to prevent the improper use of tax-exempt funds to finance a lecture course critics say was partisan, and that he misled House investigators about this.
It seemed likely he would face at least a reprimand, the third most severe penalty available, later this month.
And this is only the latest of his problems.

His often harsh pursuit of conservative Republican reform proposals, many embedded in a so-called "Contract with America," enabled Democrats to demonise him in this year's election campaign as a heartless elitist who wanted to slash Medicare health insurance for the elderly and disabled.
Some Republicans shunned him in their own campaigns.

The Medicare attacks and two partial shutdowns of the U.S. government in a budget dispute with President Bill Clinton last winter -- for which many voters blamed the Republicans -- helped reduce the party's House majority in the election.
The result is a new kinder, gentler Gingrich who has ceded much of his high-profile leadership role to Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi, an old, congenial ally.

Only Monday, before leaving Georgia to return to Washington and fight for re-election, he forecast a brave new world of accord between him and Clinton, Republicans and Democrats on key issues like budget-balancing and tax cuts.

That from an 18-year congressman who has made his name as a House "bomb-thrower" and ethics warrior since he entered the House in 1978. He helped to force the resignation of Democratic Speaker Jim Wright on ethics charges in 1989, a feat many Democrats have never forgotten or forgiven.

With fame as speaker since 1995 has come his own heavy doses of controversy. He accepted a $4.5 million advance for his book, "To Renew America," then bowed to widespread criticism and turned down the advance.
And Democrats who recall his protrayals of Congress as "corrupt" under their rule and his role in Wright's downfall have filed many ethics complaints against him.
Most were dismissed, some led to letters of mild rebuke, and two are the foundation of his current problems.
Gingrich was born June 17, 1943, in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. He is married and has two grown daughters from a first marriage that ended in divorce.
